name: Amira Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for talking with me, Amira. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and nothing you say will carry your name. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a skip lorry for Brandt's, a family skip-hire firm that's been in town for forty years. I drop empty skips at houses and building jobs, and pick up full ones with the hook arm, then tip them at the recycling yard. Maybe twelve lifts a day. People don't expect a woman to swing a full skip onto the back, so I quite enjoy their faces.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm married to Yusuf, who's a self-employed plasterer, and we rent a small house near the mosque on Station Road. We'd like children in a couple of years, God willing, but we've got less than a month saved. I use AI now and then, mostly to help Yusuf write quotes and invoices. Mr Brandt, the owner, still does the bookings on a paper diary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. People always get excited about the next big thing. I'd say it to my sisters and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, things carry on as they are. Brandt's is steady, people always need skips, and Mr Brandt looks after his drivers. The trouble is the money: my pay's lower than the big waste firms, and Yusuf's work comes and goes with the weather. We're not in danger, but we can't get ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Brandt's, maybe ask for a few Saturday lifts for extra. Yusuf and I would set up a savings pot for when the baby comes. I'd keep using the AI for his invoices, because it saves him an evening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the job, uneasy about money. It's steady but tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your household when Yusuf's work dries up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last January he had three weeks with no jobs because of the frost, and plaster won't dry in the cold. We lived on my wage and borrowed a bit from my brother. Family helps family, but I didn't like asking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you stay at Brandt's if the big firms pay more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because My boss, Mr Brandt, gave me a chance when nobody else would take a woman on a skip lorry. Loyalty counts. The big firms treat you like a number.

say: I'd say I'm **not surprised** the AI hype faded, because people chase new things.
I'd tell my **sisters** and leave it there.
think: **Brandt's** is steady and the owner looks after drivers.
Lower pay and Yusuf's **weather-dependent** work mean we can't get ahead.
do: Ask for **Saturday lifts** for extra money.
Start a **savings pot** for a future baby.

fieldNote: Amira's **loyalty** to a family firm shapes her choices more than pay.
Her household depends on Yusuf's **seasonal plastering** and her lower wage.

steps.text: Ask Brandt's for Saturday skip lifts for extra pay
Open a savings pot for a baby in two years
Stay on the skip lorry at the family firm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say every job changes and good workers adapt. I'd say it at family dinners when my cousins start worrying. Panic doesn't help anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the booking side at Brandt's would go online with AI, which Mr Brandt's son wants anyway. That would make the routes tighter, but skips still need a driver on a tight street. Yusuf's quotes and invoices get easier too. I don't think either of us loses work, at least not yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd help Mr Brandt's son set up the booking system, since I've used AI a bit. I'd keep saving for the baby. I'd watch the big waste firms to see if they start trialling robot lorries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little uneasy. More curious than frightened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Brandt's would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mrs Brandt, who answers the phones and does the books. She's sixty and doesn't want computers. I'd hope they find her something else to do, because she's family to them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would this change your plans for children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. If anything, it makes me want to have them before things change more. My mother says there's never a perfect time.

I'd tell worried cousins at family dinners that **panic** doesn't help anyone.
think: The **booking side** at Brandt's goes online with AI first.
Skips still need a **driver**, so neither of us loses work yet.
do: Help the owner's son set up the **AI booking** system.
Watch big waste firms for **robot lorry** trials.
S1.quote: Skips still need a driver on a tight street.
fieldNote: Amira sees AI taking **office tasks** at a family firm she trusts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to look after each other, families and communities, because the government won't be ready. I'd say it at the mosque and in the family group chat. People will need each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the office goes in 2028, and around 2031 robots can do the skips and the plastering. Robots doing the skips and the plastering by 2031 means me and my husband both. Two years is no time to save anything when you've got under a month in the bank. It would change everything about having children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put off trying for a baby until we know what's happening. I'd ask Mr Brandt if I can learn the weighbridge and yard work, in case that lasts longer. Yusuf and I would think about moving in with his parents to save rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. It feels like the future we planned is being taken away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Yusuf the night you heard this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we stay together and lean on family, like our parents did when they came here with nothing. He'd want to keep plastering till the end. I'd be the one making the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The robots come three years after the AGI. What would you do with those three years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Save hard and learn whatever I can at the yard. Maybe I'd take a course in something with people, like teaching assistant, because robots in a classroom seems far off. But three years goes quickly.

say: I'd urge **families and communities** to look after each other.
I'd say it at the **mosque** and in the family chat.
think: Robots around **2031** could do both the **skips** and the plastering.
**Two years** is no time to save with under a month banked.
do: Put off **trying for a baby** until things are clearer.
Ask to learn **yard work** at Brandt's.
feel: **Frightened** that their planned **future** is being taken away.
S2.quote: Robots doing the skips and the plastering by 2031 means me and my husband both.
fieldNote: Amira sees **both incomes** going, which reshapes her family plans.
She would lean on **family and faith community** before government.
She casts herself as the **planner** in her marriage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to prepare if you work at it. I'd tell the young ones in the family to get trades that need people. That's my practical side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, so the lorry lasts till about 2034. That's enough to have a child and think about a second job. I'd still worry about Yusuf, because plastering robots might come at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and start a part-time teaching assistant course in a year or two. We'd go ahead with a baby in two years as planned. We'd save a bit each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried but able to plan. It's not the same as the two-year one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why teaching assistant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I help at the mosque's weekend school, and the kids listen to me. It's work with people, not machines. And the hours would work with having my own children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut to pay for a course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eating out, and the holiday to see my grandmother. That one hurts. But she'd say do the course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to do it right and families should plan together. Ten years is a long time. I'd say that to my family and friends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With robots around 2039, I'd be thirty-nine. I'd have children by then, maybe two. I'd want to have moved into something safer before they're at school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd keep driving and keep saving. Start a family in a couple of years. Look at the teaching assistant course in a few years, when it fits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit worried, but mostly hopeful. There's time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change anything for Brandt's?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Brandt will retire by then and his son will run it. My boss's son loves gadgets, so I'd expect him to buy the robot lorries the moment they're cheap. That's when I'd need to be gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your future children about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn something where people need you to be there in person. And stay close to family, because that's what carries you.

I'd want something **safer** before the children start school.

Start a **family** in a couple of years.

fieldNote: Amira expects the owner's **son** to automate quickly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because both of us would be out of work as we're trying to start a family. What would help is apprenticeships and courses for people already working, and support for young families so they don't have to choose.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about women in trades. I fought to get on a skip lorry, and now they say robots will do it. I'd like the new jobs to be open to women from the start.

headlineQuote: I fought to get on a skip lorry, and now they say robots will do it.
portrait: Amira is a **27-year-old** skip lorry driver at a small family-owned skip-hire firm.
She's married to Yusuf, a **self-employed plasterer**, with under a month saved.
She values **loyalty**, family and faith, and leans on community before government.
Fast AGI makes her **delay children**, as both incomes look at risk.
With more time she'd move toward **teaching assistant** work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because both incomes go as they start a **family**.
